title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline against an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator we sampled K=200 paired tasks and ran a single shared initial generation per task with gpt-5-mini. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded − baseline). Observed outcome: baseline = 200/200 successful validator‑compliant applies, guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 across all pairs). We release the full preregistration, model/provider traces, validator traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay. We interpret the null as a ceiling effect under the chosen task/model/validator conditions and discuss consequences for future confirmatory designs that seek to demonstrate verifier/repair value.

sections.introduction:
Automating operator intent→configuration translation is an important operational lever in NetOps, but unconstrained model outputs risk introducing regressions and outages when applied at scale. A common architectural mitigation integrates a verifier (emulator/formal checker) that either blocks unsafe proposals or triggers an automated repair loop; we call this pattern generate→verify→repair (G→V→R). Prior work argues for verifier‑guided loops to improve operational reliability, but rigorous, preregistered quantification of the marginal benefit of verifier+repair versus generator‑only suggestions remains limited because results depend strongly on task distribution, generator strength, and validator coverage.
This study was preregistered before execution (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622) and executed autonomously under the supplied Master Prompt v1 (immutable archived reference provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The work was designed as a paired experiment that isolates the verifier/repair marginal effect by holding the generator output constant between arms (shared_initial_generation). Our primary research question: to what extent does an iterative G→V→R pipeline reduce regression‑causing changes (as measured by a deterministic validator) compared to accepting an LLM suggestion without verifier intervention? The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 expected G→V→R to yield a lower regression rate (absolute reduction target 0.08 from an assumed baseline 0.20).
sections.related_work: Two complementary strands of literature motivate this experiment. First, translator‑style usage of LLMs for NetOps—intent translation, configuration synthesis, and automated change plan generation—has rapidly expanded (surveys and application reports in 2024–2026 summarize architectural patterns and pitfalls). Second, verifier‑centric approaches (formal verifiers, emulators, or solver‑based change analyzers) and generate‑validate‑repair benchmark proposals argue that reliable automation requires formal checking or replayed testing before applying changes. Recent benchmark and system papers (e.g., Cornetto: a benchmark for LLM‑driven configuration repair; TypoNet: AI→translation for verifiable models; ORBIT: pragmatic agentic operational toolkits) emphasise that verification machinery and controlled change application are central to operational trust. Our investigation sits between these lines: it is a preregistered, paired, artifact‑grounded measurement of the incremental effect of verifier/repair under tightly controlled deterministic conditions (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan: The full preregistration froze the research question, the estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), sampling, exclusions, analysis plan, and retry policy. Key preregistered parameters: requested model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa); adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; K=200 tasks (planned episodes = 400 including both arms); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_model_calls = 400. Power calculation (preregistered) assumed a baseline regression rate ~0.20 and target absolute reduction 0.08 (alpha=0.05, power=0.80). The preregistration also enumerated exclusion and missingness rules and required that all artifact hashes be recorded and released.
Deterministic sampling and task set: Tasks were drawn deterministically from a synthetic, public intent pool produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. The selection procedure used SHA‑256(intent_string) sorting to ensure deterministic selection without human adjudication; the task_manifest and transformation_manifest were archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256: f1d447b7..., execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256: 79c91155...). We mandated that the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) report coverage for the task's required features for inclusion; this filter constrained the sample to intents the validator can evaluate.
Paired shared‑generation design: For each sampled intent the generator produced a single shared candidate configuration (shared_initial_generation). The baseline arm simulates accepting that suggestion (LLM‑only): the candidate is sent straight to scoring/validator. The guarded arm first runs the validator; if validator.valid==true the candidate is accepted, if false the preregistered guarded policy could invoke at most one repair call to the model (repair semantics frozen). This design isolates verifier/repair effects while keeping the generator output identical between arms. All per‑call prompts, responses, provider headers, and validator traces were recorded and hashed (see execution_manifest).
sections.results:
Execution and artifacts: The autonomous run executed as preregistered (execution manifest SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...); run timestamps: started 2026‑08‑27T11:26:03.764166Z, completed 2026‑08‑27T11:49:04.685661Z. Completed episodes = 400 (200 paired tasks). Model calls used = 200 (one shared generation per task). Provider call traces are archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json; response files are under execution/responses/*.txt and scoring/validator traces under execution/scoring/*.json. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms accounting consistency (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 in analysis manifest).
Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded): Baseline successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0). Guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0). Contingency table (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256: 7bc1bd2a...). Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00 (preregistered test). Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap parameters are in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The guarded repair loop was never invoked for any episode: aggregate repair_applied = 0 (scoring JSONs record repair_applied=false per episode). Representative per‑task scoring JSONs (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256: 3055f874...) show validator.valid=true and validator.normalized_configuration equal to the shared initial candidate for every sampled task. Because every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator, the guarded policy performed no additional model calls or blocking; model call accounting therefore shows identical provider usage across arms under these conditions.
Secondary metrics and operational accounting: The preregistered secondary estimands included median time‑to‑deploy and model‑call cost per successful apply. In this run these comparisons are degenerate because no repair or blocking occurred: guarded and baseline per‑task model_call_count = 1 (shared), and no additional latency from repairs is observed in provider traces. Provider event counts and per‑call latencies are archived for secondary inspection (execution/provider_calls/*.json; aggregated counts appear in the deterministic_reconciliation artifact).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The observed null result (absolute paired difference = 0.00 with exact p = 1.00) is a genuine, artifact‑grounded outcome of the preregistered design and the sampled tasks: the generator produced validator‑acceptable configurations for every sampled intent so the verifier/repair layer never engaged. This ceiling effect invalidates the preregistered power assumptions (which presupposed baseline failure probability ≈ 0.20) and demonstrates a crucial experimental lesson: a confirmatory demonstration of verifier/repair utility requires a task/generator distribution containing nontrivial baseline error probability or an experimental perturbation that induces generator mistakes.
Design consequences for future confirmatory studies: We highlight four non‑overlapping strategies—each consistent with the archived workflow—to ensure a nondegenerate paired comparison in future preregistrations: (1) sample from a failure‑rich pool (avoid filtering to only validator‑covered intents); (2) evaluate with weaker or multiple generator models to increase baseline error variance; (3) incorporate targeted adversarial perturbations or synthetic corruptions of generator outputs to create discordant cases; (4) redesign the estimand to measure the operational benefit of interactive generator–verifier loops (allowing generator responses to adapt to verifier feedback) rather than the marginal effect with a shared fixed candidate. Each strategy requires a corresponding preregistration amendment and new deterministic sampling to avoid researcher degrees of freedom.
Threats to validity and boundaries of inference: Internal validity: The paired, shared‑generation design rigorously isolates verifier/repair marginal effect under the preregistered assumptions; all seeds, deterministic sampling, and component versions were archived enabling exact replay. Construct validity: Our primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5; practical operational benefit depends on validator realism and whether validator.valid corresponds to real production regressions. External validity: This run used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a synthetic deterministic task pool filtered for validator coverage; results do not generalise to other models, task distributions, or production logs without new experiments. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation no longer applies after observing baseline=100%; we therefore report exact tests, bootstrap CIs, and full per‑task artifacts so readers can reanalyse with alternative estimands or subgroups.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, autonomously run paired comparison of a G→V→R pipeline against an LLM‑only suggestion pipeline on a deterministic synthetic NetOps task pool. The confirmatory result is a degenerate null: under the chosen sampling filter and generator, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator (200/200 successes in both arms), leaving no opportunity for verifier blocking or repair (repair_applied=0). The run is artifact‑complete and reproducible—raw prompts/responses, provider traces, validator traces, execution/analysis manifests, and hash manifests are archived—so the outcome is auditable. The operational takeaway is methodological rather than negative: demonstrating verifier/repair value in confirmatory experiments requires deliberate design to include failure‑rich inputs or weaker/perturbed generators. We release the full artifact set so future preregistered studies can build on this run’s deterministic pipeline, avoid ceiling effects, and target practical operational conditions where verifier/repair machinery can meaningfully change outcomes.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) — external validity to production change intents is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
